title: Looking for honest testers for an AI chart-analysis tool
author: Brief_Chain7348
selftext:
Hi everyone,

I’m building **CandleClarity AI**, a free educational tool that analyzes uploaded trading-chart screenshots and explains:

* Market bias and the reasoning behind it
* Support and resistance levels
* Visible indicators and patterns
* What would confirm or invalidate a setup
* What actually happened afterward

I’m looking for honest feedback not promotion or positive reviews.  
I’d especially like to know:

* Did it detect the correct asset and timeframe?
* Was the explanation understandable?
* Was anything inaccurate or misleading?
* What would make the tool genuinely useful to you?
* After Your Experience With **CandleClarity** Is There Anything That You Want A Feature To Be Removed, Improved or Added? 

If the moderators permit it, I’ll share the beta link in the comments. Thank you!

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
One thing worth settling before testers can answer your accuracy question. If the tool reads bias and levels from the same screenshot it then tells you what happened afterward from, a tester cannot tell whether the analysis was good or whether the outcome was already visible in the image, or inferable the moment it has the ticker and the date.

Cropping the chart at the decision bar and only revealing the rest after the reasoning is written would make that feedback mean something.

When it names support and resistance, is it reading those off the pixels, or pulling the real series once it identifies the asset? Those two fail in quite different ways.

replies.author: Brief_Chain7348
replies.body: Good point. CandleClarity reads bias and levels from the screenshot pixels, while live market data is added separately after identifying the asset and exchange. Its outcome tracker locks the original analysis and checks those levels against prices collected later and You’re right that old screenshots can leak future information, so historical results won’t be treated as reliable accuracy tests. I’m planning a blind mode that hides candles after a selected decision point, locks the analysis, then reveals and scores the outcome.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Then the only clean test is forward only. Stamp the analysis when it gets submitted, score it against prices that did not exist yet, and drop everything submitted off an old chart. Will testers be able to see which of their results came from live submissions versus pasted history?

replies.author: Brief_Chain7348
replies.body: You’re right. I’ll label every result as either **Live forward test** or **Historical/uncertain excluded**. Only analyses timestamped and locked before future prices exist will count toward accuracy. Testers will see the label on each result and separate statistics in their history.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The label does most of the work. One more thing to lock at submission: the levels and the bias text themselves, so nobody can edit the reasoning afterward and still have it count as live. A hash stored beside the timestamp is enough.

How long after submission does a call get scored, a fixed horizon or when price reaches a level?

replies.author: Brief_Chain7348
replies.body: Agreed. I’ll lock the timestamp, bias, levels and reasoning with a hash so edited results cannot count. Scoring will happen when price reaches the original confirmation or invalidation level; if neither is reached before a fixed deadline, it will be marked unresolved.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Two details will decide whether the accuracy number means anything. Unresolved has to stay in the denominator, otherwise a system that mostly times out looks accurate on the few that resolve. And define reached: a wick touching the invalidation level versus a close through it scores very differently. Which one are you taking?

replies.author: Brief_Chain7348
replies.body: I’m taking the stricter approach. unresolved calls stay in the denominator, and a level only counts when a candle closes beyond it on the analyzed timeframe. A wick touching the level will be recorded but won’t confirm or invalidate the call.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Close beyond on the analyzed timeframe also settles the deadline unit for you. Count it in bars of that frame rather than hours, or a 4h call and a 5m call get very different numbers of chances to resolve. And since wick touches get recorded anyway, you can publish both counts later and testers see exactly what the strict rule costs.

replies.author: Brief_Chain7348
replies.body: Agreed that’s how it now works. The deadline is 24 completed candles on the analyzed timeframe, not a fixed number of hours. A result is scored only when a candle closes beyond the locked level. Wick touches are stored separately, so later I can compare strict close-based results with touch-based results transparently.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Storing the wick touches separately is the right call. One more field worth logging: which candle number resolved it. A level closed through on candle 2 and one on candle 23 both count as hits, but they say very different things about the call, and it makes the 24 cutoff defensible when someone asks why not 30.

replies.author: Brief_Chain7348
replies.body: Good suggestion. I’ll log the resolution candle number as well for example, confirmed on candle 2 or invalidated on candle 23. That will let us measure not only whether a call resolved, but how quickly it resolved, and use the actual distribution to decide whether the 24-candle cutoff should remain or change.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
The ones that hit candle 24 are censored, not resolved, so a median over only the resolved calls will read short.

Cheaper check: resolution rate per candle. Still flat at 22 and 23 means the cutoff is truncating live calls. Near zero means 24 is fine. Are you counting invalidated and confirmed in the same distribution?
